newsitem.title: USA: Engine makers should weather Boeing deal - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Engine makers should weather Boeing deal - analysts.

text.p: The aviation industry's Big Three engine-makers should not expect any turbulence in the wake of the giant Boeing-McDonnell Douglas linkup, industry analysts said on Monday.

All three manufacturers -- General Electric Co, U.K.-based Rolls-Royce and Pratt & Whitney, a unit of Hartford-based United Technologies Corp -- could potentially benefit from the historic alliance, they said.
Boeing and McDonnell Douglas stunned the industry on Sunday by announcing a $13.3 billion merger that will see Boeing absorb McDonnell.

"This makes the entire industry healthier, the fact that McDonnell Douglas's future is no longer in question," said Michael Bunyaner, senior vice president at Oppenheimer & Co. "Therefore it will be positive for engine-makers."
Bunyaner emphasized that the engine business was distinct from the aircraft business.
"Engines are sold directly to airlines and are priced separately. Airlines choose which planes they will add to their fleet and engine-makers don't care," he said.

"I don't see it making a big difference (to engine-makers), because McDonnell Douglas was already such a minor player," said another Wall Street analyst. "If McDonnell had merged with Airbus, it would be a much different story."

"It's definitely good for engine-makers," said Nicholas Heyman, analyst at NatWest Securities Corp. With fewer aircraft makers, the engine companies "will spend less effort to try to outdo each other."
"It means reduced risk for nominal return, new-engine programs and enhanced returns for most entrenched engine manufacturers on existing airframes," he said.
Another analyst said: "You've now got one mammoth customer in the U.S. for engines -- Boeing."
General Electric, with its strong ties to Boeing as exclusive supplier of 737 engines (along with GE's French partner SNECMA), stood to benefit the most, said one analyst.
"It's good news for GE, because they already had such a strong relationship with Boeing and McDonnell Douglas," said Bill Fiala, aerospace analyst at Edward D. Jones in St. Louis.
He pointed out that McDonnell President Harry Stonecipher formerly ran GE Aircraft Engines.
Fiala said Pratt & Whitney was also well-positioned.
"They're the deepest in having the broadest product line. They're not as dependent on any one product or manufacturer and with that diversity comes some safety."

Fiala said Pratt was still in a good position because its engines will be used by both Boeing and Lockheed Martin in the competition for the U.S. Joint Strike Fighter contract. Spokesmen for Pratt and GE both told Reuters on Monday that it was too early to assess the merger's impact, but they hoped to continue their good relations with Boeing and McDonnell.
Pratt separately announced a massive contract from South Korea's Asiana Airlines on Monday to supply engines for 48 new Airbus Industrie A330 and Boeing 777 aircraft over the next 10 years.
Industry analysts said the contract was probably worth about $1 billion.
